steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Induction training introduces new employees to the business: health and safety, company culture, policies, and basic procedures. It helps new starters settle in quickly and feel valued.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: On-the-job training: learning by doing the actual job, guided by an experienced colleague or mentor. It's practical, relevant, and cheap, but the trainer may pass on bad habits and production may slow during training.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Off-the-job training: learning away from the workplace (college courses, workshops, online programmes). It provides broader skills and professional qualifications, but is more expensive and may not be directly relevant to the specific job.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Training benefits: improved skills and productivity, better quality, fewer mistakes and accidents, increased motivation (shows investment in staff), and greater flexibility (multi-skilled workforce can cover different roles).

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Explain the difference between on-the-job and off-the-job training, giving one advantage and one disadvantage of each. | Analyse how training can improve a business's competitiveness. | Evaluate whether a business should train its existing staff or recruit new employees who already have the required skills.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always link training to specific business outcomes: productivity, quality, motivation, competitiveness. When evaluating training, consider the COST vs the RETURN: training is an investment, not just an expense. Don't forget: trained staff may leave - this is a key drawback to address in evaluation questions.
